The sole difficulty that appeared to occupy him was the choice of whom to dispatch. He understood perfectly that murder, like the faiths of the Pagan world, demands a victim no less than a priest. Since he was no genius, he possessed no enemies; moreover, he considered this an unsuitable occasion for indulging private resentment or aversion, his undertaking being of the utmost gravity and solemnity. He therefore wrote the names of his friends and relations upon a sheet of notepaper and, after deliberate reflection, selected Lady Clementina Beauchamp. This dear elderly lady lived in Curzon Street and was his second cousin on his mother's side. He had always cherished Lady Clem, as she was universally known. Being himself extremely rich, having inherited the whole of Lord Rugby's estate upon attaining his majority, he could gain no sordid financial benefit from her death. Indeed, the longer he considered it, the more perfectly she seemed to meet the requirements. Any postponement would be unjust to Sybil, he felt, and he resolved to arrange matters immediately.

Naturally, his first business was to pay the cheiromantist. Seating himself at a little Sheraton desk near the window, he wrote a cheque for £105 to Mr. Septimus Podgers, sealed it in an envelope, and instructed his valet to deliver it to West Moon Street. Next he telephoned the stables for his hansom and dressed for an outing. At the door he turned to look at Sybil Merton's photograph, vowing that whatever happened, she would never learn what he was undertaking for her. The secret of his self-sacrifice would remain forever within his own heart.

On the road to the Buckingham he called at a florist's and ordered for Sybil a lovely basket of narcissus, their white petals surrounding bright pheasant's eyes. Reaching the club, he proceeded directly to the library, rang, and requested that the waiter bring a lemon-and-soda and a volume on Toxicology. He had settled firmly upon poison as the most suitable means of conducting this disagreeable business. Any personal violence was profoundly repugnant to him. Besides, he particularly wished to avoid murdering Lady Clementina in a fashion likely to draw public notice. The prospect of becoming a celebrity at Lady Windermere's, or finding his name displayed in the paragraphs of vulgar society newspapers, was hateful to him.

So I went to the plantation and began questioning the older Black residents again. Eventually, one of the oldest women said she had heard of a place called Bessop's Castle and thought she could lead me there. It was neither a castle nor a tavern, she explained, but a tall rock.

"I offered to pay her well for helping me. After some hesitation, she agreed to take me. We found the place easily enough, and once I had sent her away, I began examining it. The 'castle' was an irregular group of cliffs and rocks. One rock stood out because of its great height and its isolated, almost man-made appearance. I climbed to the top, then found myself unsure what to do next.

"While I stood thinking, I noticed a narrow shelf on the rock's eastern side, perhaps a yard below the summit. It stuck out about eighteen inches and was no more than a foot wide. A hollow in the cliff just above it made the whole thing look roughly like one of the hollow-backed chairs our ancestors used. I felt certain this was the 'devil's seat' mentioned in the manuscript. Suddenly the entire riddle seemed to make sense.

"The 'good glass' could only mean a telescope. Sailors rarely use the word 'glass' in any other way. I immediately understood that the instructions called for looking through a telescope from one exact position, with no room to vary it. I was equally sure that 'forty-one degrees and thirteen minutes' and 'northeast and by north' told me how to aim it. Greatly excited by these discoveries, I hurried home, found a telescope, and returned to the rock.

"I lowered myself onto the shelf and discovered that only one sitting position allowed me to stay there. This supported my earlier conclusion. I began using the telescope. Clearly, 'forty-one degrees and thirteen minutes' described the angle above the visible horizon, since 'northeast and by north' already gave the horizontal direction. I found that direction immediately with a pocket compass. Then I pointed the telescope upward at what I guessed to be an angle of forty-one degrees and carefully moved it up and down. At last I noticed a round opening in the leaves of a large, distant tree that rose above the others around it.

I uncovered it, and a light breeze quickly stirred it into flame. Noticing this, I made a fan from branches and used it to revive the embers whenever they nearly died out. When darkness returned, I was pleased to discover that the fire provided light as well as warmth. It also proved useful for food: some scraps left by the travellers had been roasted and tasted much better than the berries I gathered from trees. I therefore tried cooking my own food by laying it directly on the glowing embers. This ruined the berries, but greatly improved the nuts and roots.

"Food soon grew scarce, however. Often I spent an entire day searching unsuccessfully for a few acorns to ease my hunger. I decided to leave the place where I had been living and look for somewhere that could satisfy my few needs more easily. The prospect of losing my fire distressed me greatly. I had found it by chance and did not know how to create another. For several hours I considered this problem seriously, but at last I had to give up trying to solve it. Wrapping myself in my cloak, I set off through the woods toward the setting sun. I wandered for three days before finally reaching open countryside. Heavy snow had fallen the previous night, covering the fields in an unbroken white sheet. The view was desolate, and the cold, wet substance on the ground chilled my feet.

"It was about seven in the morning, and I desperately wanted food and shelter. At last I noticed a small hut on a rise, evidently built for a shepherd's use. I had never seen anything like it and studied its construction with great curiosity. The door stood open, so I went inside. An old man sat beside a fire, preparing his breakfast over it. Hearing a sound, he turned and saw me. He screamed, fled the hut, and raced across the fields faster than his frail body seemed capable of moving. His appearance, unlike any I had seen before, and his sudden flight puzzled me somewhat. But the hut itself enchanted me. Neither rain nor snow could enter; the ground was dry. At that moment it seemed as beautiful and heavenly a refuge to me as Pandemonium must have seemed to the demons of hell after their suffering in the lake of fire.
